Learning from sensor data
A small research team is building a system that helps a greenhouse operator understand changes in temperature and humidity. The operator records measurements every minute, but reviewing each measurement takes too much time. The software should describe unusual patterns without changing the original records. Its output is advice for a person, not an instruction to control heating equipment automatically. A prediction is not a guarantee that a future event will happen. The interface must distinguish observations from predictions and explain when information is missing. Before selecting a model, the team checks whether measurements use consistent units. A temperature written in degrees Celsius cannot be compared directly with a temperature written in degrees Fahrenheit. The team also checks timestamps because a missing hour must not be interpreted as an hour with zero humidity. Several sensors have different sampling intervals, so records are aligned before analysis. No original measurement is overwritten during preparation. A separate dataset contains the prepared values and a reference to each source record. Each transformation is documented so another developer can reproduce it. The team keeps unusual examples for manual review, including a disconnected sensor, a rapidly changing temperature, and a day with no measurements. A missing value must remain distinguishable from a valid measurement of zero. The operator can reject a recommendation and inspect the supporting observations. These decisions provide feedback, but they do not automatically become verified training labels. Someone must first check whether a decision reflects a real event, an equipment problem, or a misunderstanding. The team records the model version used for every prediction. When a new model is introduced, old results remain associated with the version that produced them. This makes comparisons possible without pretending that different models are identical. A summary should mention relevant observations, but it must not invent explanations for events that the data cannot establish. If processing fails, the original measurements must still be available. The project succeeds only if the operator understands both the results and their limitations. Faster processing alone does not establish better quality, and a confident explanation can still be wrong. For that reason, the team reviews examples from several seasons before deciding whether the system is ready for everyday use. The winter evaluation includes cold mornings and long periods of artificial lighting. The summer evaluation includes warm afternoons and rapidly changing ventilation settings. A model that performs well in one season may behave differently in another. The operator therefore receives a short explanation of the evaluation conditions alongside the results. No statement about a season should be added unless the corresponding measurements exist. The reviewer also checks whether a warning was repeated unnecessarily, because repeated warnings can hide a genuinely new event. These requirements are recorded before the final evaluation begins, and they remain unchanged while the team compares candidate models.

Classification
Binary classification assigns an observation to one of two classes, such as ordinary or unusual. Multiclass classification allows more than two classes. Here, additional classes describe a disconnected sensor, an unexpected temperature change, and an invalid timestamp. These are different conditions rather than successive processing stages.

Training and evaluation
Supervised learning uses labeled training data. The team separates training data from test data before adjusting the model. Validation data helps compare settings, including the learning rate. A low training error does not prove that a model works well on new observations. Overfitting can improve results on familiar records while reducing performance on unseen records.
- Read the original measurements and preserve
  the distinction between missing values and zero.
- Compare predictions with reviewed labels before
  publishing an evaluation report.
1) Record the model version and evaluation settings.
2) Keep the test dataset separate from the training dataset.

Retrieval and generation
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines document retrieval with text generation. Maintenance documentation provides context for an explanation, but retrieved text does not automatically prove that an explanation is correct. A reviewer checks whether the instructions actually apply to the device involved.

Final review
The dataset contains 1,250 records. Processing takes 2.5 seconds and uses 8 GB of memory. Accuracy increases from 90% to 95%, an increase of five percentage points. Do not overwrite the source file. If an explanation cannot be translated, preserve its original text and record its location. The final report must include this closing requirement rather than ending after the first successful section.
